title: "The Abstract Reasoning Gap: Human vs. Machine"
author: "Audrey Tsung"

Recent headlines about autonomous AI agents executing real-world cyber breaches make it easy to feel like agentic ai is something within reach. It can feel really daunting without any understanding of the underlying capabilities and limitations. That tension between alarming headlines and actual benchmark rigor is why I chose this dataset. As the race for agentic AI intensifies, it's crucial to separate the signal from the noise.

Whenever a lab claims a model has "surpassed human performance," my immediate reaction is skepticism: *Which humans, and evaluated under what conditions?*

 While marketing hype treats the "human baseline" as a monolithic gold standard, the reality ranges from IMO gold medalists to crowdworkers who gave up on 70% of the problems.

My goal for this post is to dig into item-level ConceptARC data, benchmarking 482 human testers against machine solvers on the exact same abstract reasoning tasks. A decision tree might seem simplistic compared to modern large language models, but training one across 16 cognitive concepts cuts through the noise. It lets us map exactly where the "superhuman" narrative holds up, and where human intuition still wins.

## Data Source & Pre-processing

This analysis utilizes item-level test data from the [AI Benchmarks vs Human Baselines](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kylefengkfeng209/ai-benchmarks-vs-human-baselines) dataset. We examine `conceptarc_human_vs_machine.csv`, which records success rates across 528 identical abstract reasoning tasks.
